title: AI-enhanced LVSim2.0 technology for rapid phenotypic susceptibility testing of new and experimental TB drugs
text:
Tuberculosis (TB) and multidrug-resistant TB continue threatening global public heath, causing over 10 million
illnesses and 1.5 million deaths each year. The project will develop a simple, integrated system that can rapidly
determine if TB is susceptible or resistant to new TB drugs. Since we currently lack molecular or commercial
assays for monitoring and determining emerging resistance to new TB drugs, this technology enables rapid
determination of appropriate drug treatment for patients with multidrug-resistant TB disease.

title: Integration of Basal Ganglia and Cerebellar Outputs in Motor Control and Parkinson's Disease
text:
Parkinson’s disease disrupts motor control not only through basal ganglia dysfunction but through broader
circuit-level disturbances involving the cerebellum and thalamus. This project will identify how these motor
pathways converge in the thalamus, how their integration supports normal movement, and how it breaks down
in Parkinsonian states. By defining these mechanisms and testing circuit-based interventions, this work aims to
reveal new therapeutic strategies that restore coordinated motor function in Parkinson’s disease.

title: Novel cell therapy approaches for molecularly defined subsets of therapy-resistant melanoma
text:
Although some patients have durable disease control with current cancer immunotherapies, many fail to
respond or progress after initially experiencing tumor regression. This proposal seeks to develop new,
mechanism-based cellular immunotherapies to target melanoma and other common cancers with specific
genetic alterations associated with resistance to current treatments. As part of these studies, new
generalizable knowledge will be generated that improves our molecular understanding of how the adaptive
immune system can distinguish between normal and transformed tissues.

title: New technologies for imaging of the human cochlea
text:
Inner ear diseases can have a major impact on a person's quality of life. However, current medical imaging
methods lack the resolution needed to visualize the tiny structures inside the cochlea and are unable to
measure their motion or function. The technology we are developing aims to solve this problem by advancing
optical coherence tomography as a high-resolution imaging tool for the human inner ear.

title: Molecular mechanisms of TAK1 regulation in rheumatoid arthritis
text:
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic inflammatory disease, which results in inflammation of the synovial lining
and destruction of the adjacent bone and cartilage mediated by RA synovial fibroblasts. In this proposal, we aim
to examine the therapeutic importance of TGFβ-activated kinase 1 (TAK1) inhibitors in synovial fibroblasts
isolated from RA patient-donated tissues, and in a mouse collagen-antibody-induced arthritis (CAIA) model. Our
work will provide a rationale for therapeutically targeting this kinase for the management of synovial hyperplasia,
inflammation, and tissue destruction in RA.

title: Program stem-like CD8 T cells to enhance antiviral immunity against chronic viral infection
text:
Chronic viral infections affect millions of people worldwide and post a major public health challenge. This
proposal aims to identify the molecular and cellular mechanisms required for long-term antiviral CD8 T-cell
immunity and efficacy of immunotherapy against chronic viral infection. The results from this study will unveil
novel targets that can be harnessed to induce durable control of chronic viral infection in patients.

title: 1/2 The Partnership for Native American Cancer Prevention
text: The overarching goals and objectives of the Partnership for Native American Cancer Prevention (NACP) are to reduce the cancer burden within the Arizona AIAN population through research and community engagement, expand the number of investigators working in cancer research, and increase the total number of investigators focused on AIAN cancer health. NACP will embrace the two eyed seeing paradigm which seeks to see from one eye with the strengths of AIAN community perspectives and from the other eye with the strengths of contemporary scientific perspectives, and to use both of these eyes together for the benefit of all.

title: Understanding the persistence of Dengue epidemic and associated risk factors in Urban Bamako Mali
text: Dengue fever disease (DFD) is rapidly expanding in Mali, where active transmission provides a unique and essential setting to study dengue virus (DENV) evolution, transmission, and severity. This project will generate genomic, epidemiologic, and immunologic evidence that improves dengue diagnosis, surveillance, and outbreak response. By building sustainable diagnostic and genomic capacity in Mali, the work enhances global health security and provides actionable intelligence that informs U.S. travel medicine, vaccine strategy, and public health readiness—maximizing the impact of NIH’s international research

title: Regulation of mesoderm fate patterning through multiscale dynamics
text:
Early human development hinges on the dynamic interplay of cellular behaviors shaped by the surrounding
milieu. This project investigates how cell migration molds these environments, fostering tissue diversity and
complexity crucial for both regeneration and disease contexts. These insights will provide valuable pathways
for understanding and manipulating cell behavior in tissue development, wound healing, and disease
progression.

title: Redesigning HBV Assembly Capsid Modulators to Induce Apoptosis
text:
Chronic Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) is a silent epidemic affecting about 300 million people worldwide
and 2 million in the United States; chronic HBV leads to almost a million deaths each year from
liver failure, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. A subset of Capsid Assembly Modulators
(CAMs), which inhibit self-assembly of infectious viruses, have shown the potential to specifically
lead HBV-infected cell to programmed cell death (apoptosis), a means of clearing the host of
infected cells. Here we propose a rational approach to improved CAM design to emphasize an
apoptotic outcome.

title: Aberrant Glycogen in Lung Adenocarcinoma Tumorigenesis
text:
Diagnosis of non-precision medicine targetable lung cancer represents a bleak future with lower chance of
survival and a poor quality of life. For many lung cancer patients, the only treatment options available are
traditional multi-agent chemotherapy coupled with surgery and/or radiation. This project will explore the
pathogenic roles of glycogen in lung cancer biology and progression and drive the discovery of personalized
therapies that can be leveraged for the lung cancer patients that only qualify for conventional chemotherapy.

title: Mass Spectrometry and Analytical Pharmacology Shared Resource
text: MASS SPECTROMETRY & ANALYTICAL PHARMACOLOGY SHARED RESOURCE: PROJECT SUMMARY In 2021, the Proteomics & Metabolomics Shared Resource (PMSR), which had been Cancer Center Support Grant (CCSG)–funded since 2009, was reorganized to form the Mass Spectrometry & Analytical Pharmacology Shared Resource (MSAPSR) with the inclusion of new mass spectrometry imaging (MSI), pharmacokinetic (PK), and pharmacodynamics (PD) capabilities at the NJ site. The MSAPSR functions under a collaborative model organized into four essential components: (1) proteomics, (2) metabolomics, (3) molecular imaging, and (4) PK/PD applications. The creation of MSAPSR affords Georgetown Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center (LCCC) Members seamless access to cutting-edge technical expertise, services, and technologies across the consortium. MSAPSR is co-directed by Claire Carter, PhD (NJ), Junfeng Ma, PhD (DC) and Amrita Cheema, PhD (DC), and is supported by five staff members and two faculty members with expertise in sample preparation, experimental design, data acquisition and data analysis. Supported by $6.9M in institutional investment since 2019, MSAPSR houses multiple state-of-the-art instruments across both campuses to provide: (1) routine and advanced MS -based proteomic studies for the identification of proteins and peptides, and the characterization of post-translational modifications (phosphorylation, acetylation, O-GlcNAcylation) and quantification (iTRAQ); (2) multiplex and spatial imaging of protein markers at the subcellular level using imaging mass cytometry (IMC) for cancer cells and immune cells in tissue sections; (3) comprehensive metabolomic and lipidomic profiling and quantitation, through the utilization of over a dozen in-house developed and validated MS-based assays; (4) real-time cellular metabolic flux and respiration analysis using the Seahorse Extracellular Flux Analyzer; (5) MSI to allow untargeted label-free imaging of lipids, metabolites, glycans, peptides and pharmaceuticals within tissue sections and 3D organoid/spheroid models; and (6) support for drug development pipelines through MS-based PK and PD investigations. The MSAPSR receives input from the Advisory Committee and annual user surveys to prioritize development and assess programmatic needs across the Consortium. To this end, the individual components of the MSAPSR augment basic, clinical, translational, and population science cancer research by providing access to the expertise and instrumentation for a wide spectrum of MS- based molecular phenotyping services. Taken together, these components support systems biology understanding of the interplay between pathways that drive cancer development, aggression, metastatic disease, resistance to therapy and therapeutic efficacy. In FY2022, the MSAPSR provided services to 28 LCCC Members across all three LCCC Research Programs (10 Cancer Cell Biology Members, 16 Cancer Host Interactions Members, and 2 Cancer Prevention and Control Members). During the current project period, the MSAPSR enabled the success of 31 peer-reviewed cancer-relevant extramural grants, 3 clinical trials and 54 peer-reviewed publications, including 10 publications in high-impact (IF >10) journals.

title: Explainable and Ethical AI for Studying Alzheimer's Disease
text:
Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is rapidly transforming into a significant economic and social challenge. This
proposal will develop and apply advanced AI models to study Alzheimer’s Disease, including the effects of
race, comorbidity, and social determinant of health on Alzheimer’s Disease as well as identifying cerebrospinal
fluid proteins that are predictive of cognitive decline. Successful completion of this study will provide improved
and fair AI models that can be further developed into effective clinical decision support tools as well as
enhance our understanding of the pathophysiology of AD.

title: Intratumoral microbiota and immune predictors of response to immunotherapy in lung cancer
text:
Although immunotherapy has become the first line of therapy in advanced patients with lung cancer, less than
half of all eligible patients respond to immunotherapy. In this grant, we will uncover intratumoral microbial and
immunological predictors that distinguish responders from non-responders, with the goal of identifying new
targets for more effective immunotherapies. In clinical practice, these predictors could help optimize patient
selection for treatment with immunotherapy and facilitate the development of precision immunotherapy.

title: Advancing the commercialization readiness of nanoparticle-based immunotherapy for cancer treatment
text:
Lung cancer is by far the leading cause of cancer deaths in the US and worldwide; standard chemo and
radiation therapy is not widely effective, and less than 20% of patients respond to immunotherapy. In the
parent fast-track SBIR grant, we develop a next generation immunotherapy, based on nanoparticle co-delivery
of a potent anti-cancer RNA, an immune checkpoint inhibitor, and an immune-stimulating agent, that will lead
to antitumor immune response and curative outcomes in advanced lung cancer patients. This grant will
enhance our commercialization readiness by supporting intellectual property protection of the technology in the
US and abroad and initiating regulatory-compliant manufacturing of our drug loaded nanoparticles.

title: Evaluating the role of the tumor macroenvironment in cancer cachexia
text:
Cancer cachexia is a debilitating syndrome affecting many cancer patients, leading to severe muscle and fat
loss, decreased quality of life, poorer treatment response, and higher mortality rates2
, This research aims to
uncover the mechanisms through which tumors and their microenvironments drive cachexia by disrupting
systemic metabolism, with a particular focus on their interactions with critical metabolic regulatory organs (i.e.
the TMaE). By identifying novel therapeutic targets, this work has the potential to improve treatment outcomes,
well-being, and survival for cancer patients, addressing a critical public health need.

title: Investigating the Heterogeneous Intercellular Signaling of Hematopoietic Stem and Progenitor Cells and its Changes around the Circadian Clock
text:
Hematopoietic stem cells are responsible for life-long blood regeneration and, as such, are regarded as the
most important cell types for regenerative medicine. The proposed research will study how cell-cell
communication in the bone marrow regulates the production of blood and immune cells and how cell-cell
signaling changes around the circadian clock. Potential findings can help understand physiological response to
bleeding, infection, and disease, and may reveal new therapeutic targets for blood and immune disorders.

title: Live-cell Activity Architecture in Cancer
text:
The overall goal of our research is to provide a better understanding of how cancer cells
misinterpret or ignore signals that normally tell cells to stop dividing or begin suicide, leading to
uncontrolled tumor growth. We will also develop novel assays to facilitate the development of
new cancer therapeutics.

title: Improving inferences on health effects of chemical exposures
text:
Humans are exposed to a complex mixture of chemicals through their environment, and it is of
critical public health importance to assess how these exposures impact human health and risk
of adverse outcomes. However, it is very challenging to disentangle the health effects of the
different exposures due to dimensionality, nonlinearities, interactions and high correlation.
This project develops transformative new tools for obtaining interpretable inferences on
exposure effects for both mixtures and toxicological screening.

title: Identifying arginylation inhibitors to attenuate injury-induced neuronal cell death
text:
This study aims to identify novel small molecules that selectively inhibit the arginylation activity of
arginyltransferase 1 with low cellular toxicity and favorable membrane permeability, for future potential use in
reducing secondary injury–induced cell death following spinal cord injury in humans.
